Colouring a heading because it looks nice.
Colouring a warning in red.

questions.stem: Why is a comic-style typeface inappropriate for a planning memo?

answer.exemplar: A comic-style typeface signals informality and playfulness, undermining the authority and professionalism expected in a planning document.

questions.learningObjective: Place images to break up long text blocks.
questions.stem: Which image placement best breaks up a long text block in a memo?

options.text: An image placed before any text.
An image placed only at the very end.
An image placed in the footer.
An image placed mid-paragraph to split the block.

questions.explanation: Placing an image mid-paragraph splits long text and aids scanning. End or footer placement does not break the block.

questions.learningObjective: Use whitespace to create a visual hierarchy.

stimulus.body: The memo uses large gaps before headings and small gaps before body paragraphs. Readers navigate easily.

questions.stem: Why does the spacing strategy work?

options.text: It makes headings smaller.
It wastes space before headings.
It creates a visual hierarchy that signals importance.
It hides body paragraphs.

questions.explanation: Larger gaps before headings signal importance and create hierarchy. The gaps are functional, not wasteful.

questions.learningObjective: Recognise when type size hierarchy is flat.

stimulus.body: The memo sets headings at 11 pt and body text at 10.5 pt. Readers cannot distinguish levels.

questions.stem: What causes the indistinguishable levels?

options.text: The colours are too similar.

The type size hierarchy is too flat.

questions.learningObjective: Apply all layout principles to a memo image and caption.
questions.stem: Which option best combines grid alignment, caption proximity, and whitespace?

options.text: The image floats freely with a distant caption and no surrounding space.
